g.text: CAPSTONE 01
DoseDay
Desk Research, IA & Flows, Wireframes
1ST PAGE · DISCOVERY
EVIDENCE BASE · 8 SOURCES, ALL LINK-CHECKED 2026-09-26
competitor + analog
articles + reports
real user reviews
App Store / Play / Reddit
AI claims hand-checked
cut as unsupported
Every review is quoted with username
and date. Vendor-selected testimonials
are recorded but never counted.
1 · Competitor and analog products
screenshots captured from store listings
01 · MEDISAFE — DIRECT, FREEMIUM
4.7 / 5 · ~100K ratings
KEY FLOW, AS ADVERTISED
add medication → schedule dose times →
push reminder → mark taken → repeat
ALSO SELLING
HealthKit sync · shareable PDF for a doctor ·
"family interaction" for a whole family on one
account · refill reminders · selectable
reminder sounds ("Medtones")
The app's own pitch leads with shared family
access, not the single user's dose.
apps.apple.com/us/app/medisafe-medication-management
02 · MYTHERAPY — DIRECT, FREEMIUM
KEY FLOW, AS ADVERTISED
add medication (tablet, drop, injection,
vitamin) → set reminder → confirm or skip →
see streaks and a monthly report
ALSO SELLING
refill alerts · health journal with symptom and
pain diary · measurements · "family profiles
for shared care"
"Motivation with Streaks to stay consistent" is
advertised as a headline benefit. See F-8.
apps.apple.com/us/app/pill-reminder-mytherapy
03 · HERO — HARDWARE + SUBSCRIPTION
$29.99 / month + a physical dispenser
KEY FLOW, PER VENDOR WALKTHROUGH
install app → activate subscription → set
schedule and dose per medication → load a
90-day supply → dispenser sorts, locks and
dispenses only the correct dose
HARD CONSTRAINT, THEIR OWN COPY
"requires an active Hero subscription and a
connected smart dispenser. It does not work
as a stand-alone application."
Removes the behaviour problem with hardware,
and charges $30/month for it.
herohealth.com
04 · ANALOG — THE PILL ORGANIZER AND THE TALKING PILL BOTTLE
A physical object cannot be screenshotted, so this analog is evidenced through user testimony about what they used before the app.
melanie605, App Store 11/17/2019 — "It also shows a picture of the pill so I'm grabbing the right one out of the pill case since they are all together.
Pill cases are great but not everything falls under the am, afternoon and pm schedule."
Linda Smith, Google Play 31 July 2026 — "No more filling med boxes every 2 weeks that used to take over an hour, always had an error and I would occassionally forget to take."
2 · Articles and reports
A1 · WHO, 2003 — adherence in developed countries averages about 50% for chronic-disease medicines.
who.int/news/item/01-07-2003-failure-to-take-prescribed-medicine-for-chronic-diseases
A2 · CDC, 2017 Grand Rounds — adherence barriers are multi-layered: complex dosing, side effects, cost, poor coordination, low engagement.
archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/grand-rounds/pp/2017/20170221-medication-adherence.html
A3 · PMC5694345 — common usability failures in older-adult medication apps: difficult navigation, poor visibility, inflexible reminders, too much manual entry.
pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5694345/
A4 · Frontiers in Medical Technology, 2021 — independently scored 8 apps. Every app scored full marks on "provides a reminder function".
frontiersin.org/journals/medical-technology/articles/10.3389/fmedt.2020.616242/full
3 · Top 5 findings, each tied to a named source
full detail: research/03_one_page_summary.md
F-1 · The reminder is half the product. The record is the other half.
Users are not asking to be nagged. They are asking to stop not knowing whether they already took something — and when.
SOURCES
GeekyDragonfly, App Store 05/04/2022 — "no more guessing whether I took a medicine or not … and what time I actually took it"
Meinnm505, App Store May 5 — "It took the guess work out of the equation" · LiinaLatrell, App Store Jan 19 — "This stops all that confusion"
rlsmith1994, App Store Jun 9 — "you have to mark your pills as taken … it doesn't go away if you don't take your meds"
F-2 · Reminder frequency is table stakes. Scheduling arithmetic is where products break.
All 8 apps scored by A4 earned full marks for "provides a reminder function". What breaks is any regimen that is not a clean daily time.
SOURCES
A4 (Frontiers 2021), criterion 16 — full marks across all 8 apps · SF Cavendish, App Store 11/23/2021 — "1 or 2 tablets/dose … I've given up"
MikeyBGr8, App Store 01/19/2022 — "the start and end date option doesn't take into account for the frequency"
GeekyDragonfly 05/04/2022 (2-hourly) · Linda Smith, Google Play 31 July 2026 — "My meds vary from 1x week to 3x/day"
F-3 · Interface depth is an accessibility problem, and users name the mechanism.
Reviewers do not say "too many menus". They say the people using this software may be cognitively impaired by the condition, or by the drug.
SOURCES
tuxedoyam, App Store 12/25/2021 — "people taking medications might also have some degree of brain fog or mental impairment either due to the condition or as a side effect"
andrewleesh, App Store SG 16/07/2020 — "it takes 4 taps on tiny icons over various parts of the screen"
SF Cavendish 11/23/2021 — "several separate groups … but they didn't talk to each other" · corroborated by A3 (PMC5694345)
F-4 · Reminder persistence means opposite things depending on who shares the record.
Relentless is a feature for one person on one phone, and a fault when a second carer marks the dose and the first phone keeps firing.
SOURCES
Feature side: rlsmith1994 Jun 9 · eventidephoenix, App Store 10/10/2018 — "You get multiple notifications until you take it … make it more annoying"
Fault side: 123334567, App Store 08/06/2024 — "My husband will mark something taken, I'll get reminders on my device … There's a disconnect between taken status and notifications"
The variable is not preference. It is the number of people writing to one record.
F-5 · In a medication app, reliability defects are trust defects.
Being unable to add a medication, or a reminder that silently never arrived, breaks the only thing the product is for.
SOURCES
CoastieWife74, App Store Mar 8 — "Now I have new meds to take and I can't add them to the app. I even tried deleting some and…nothing … I'll have to."
Reddit r/androidapps — "not getting notifications at one point but it was the phone's battery settings"
From the user's side, "the app is broken" and "the reminder never arrived" are indistinguishable.
4 · Claude synthesis, and where I corrected it
full output + prompt: research/02_synthesis_and_verification.md
THE PROMPT, AS SENT TO CLAUDE
Raw notes attached as a file and declared the only
permitted evidence base. Asked for four things:
1 · THEMES — 5 to 7, each with supporting IDs
2 · CONTRADICTIONS — 3 to 5, with what
distinguishes the two sides
3 · UNMET NEEDS — 5 to 8, marked UNSERVED
or BADLY SERVED
4 · WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SUPPORT
THE RULES THAT MADE IT CHECKABLE
· Cite only R1–R22, A1–A4. Never invent an ID,
quote, username, date, statistic or URL.
· Do not paraphrase a quote into a stronger claim.
One person's opinion is not a rate or a majority.
· If you cannot support it, put it in section 4.
· No invented ages, genders, titles, conditions,
market sizes or clinical outcomes.
· Section 4 vendor testimonials are NOT a sample.
· A theme under 3 review IDs must be marked WEAK.
Result: 42 claims checked by hand, 36 passed,
6 failed and were cut. Full audit in the file.
SIX PLACES CLAUDE WAS CORRECTED
V-1 · Wrong and reversed. Called Apple Health sync
UNSERVED, "nobody offers it". But Medisafe's own
listing advertises HealthKit sync, while reviewer
DAHM reports keeping two parallel records.
Reclassified: badly served and disputed.
V-2 · Overstated. Cited R1 as being "alerted" about
drugs that clash. R1 used the app's timestamp log
to work out the spacing themselves. That dropped the
theme to 2 IDs, under its own threshold.
V-3 · Wrong fit. R18 wants MORE nagging, not relief.
V-4 · Duplicate. Two of its seven themes were the
same finding. Merged into F-1.
V-5 · Misframed. R16's inability to add a medication is
a defect, not a pricing cap. Reframed as a lockout.
V-6 · Mislabelled. Cited "section 5" for the absence of
market figures. A4 does carry 2017 counts.
It also flagged one of its own themes WEAK for having
only 2 supporting reviews, and refused to promote it.
That is why the rest could be checked at all.
5 · What this evidence does not support
· No current adherence rate. The ~50% figure is WHO 2003, developed countries generally — not app users, not current. (A1)
· No market size. 325,000 mHealth apps and ~10,000 medication reminders are 2017 counts from one source. (A4)
· No willingness to pay. Hero's $29.99/month is hardware + subscription in a different category; Philips $60 and MedMinder $50
are an unverified claim on Hero's own marketing page.
· No clinical outcome. The one outcome-shaped anecdote sits in the vendor-selected set and is excluded by rule — a vendor picking
its own testimonials is not a sample.
· No "users want X" statistics. 22 self-selected reviews are 22 people. A theme with 3 supporting reviews is three people.
· No usability finding about DoseDay. It does not exist yet. Every usability point here is about a competitor or an analog.
· No interviews. The interviews/ corpus is a separate, explicitly SIMULATED practice dataset for the AI-persona pipeline. It is not
evidence for this brief and is not used anywhere on this page.
F-8 · An absence, recorded as a constraint and not as evidence: none of the 22 reviewers mentions streaks, scores or gamification in any
form — yet MyTherapy advertises "Motivation with Streaks" as a headline benefit. A broken streak punishes exactly the missed night that made our
primary user delete a good app. Zero user evidence stands behind this, and it is not counted as a finding.
6 · What the research changed, and who it is for
DESIGN RESPONSE, TRACED TO A FINDING
1 · Today leads with a record, not a countdown — "what is already done" first (F-1)
2 · Dose entry supports variable amounts and irregular frequency, incl. as-needed logging (F-2)
3 · Reminder escalation branches on whether anyone else shares the record (F-4)
4 · No streaks, no scores, no red-for-missed. A missed dose is a reversible check-in (F-8)
5 · Adding a medication can never be blocked, and a missed reminder is a state we can explain (F-5)
PRIMARY USER
Rowan, 59
rotating shift work · employer unnamed
Five medications: three scheduled, two as-needed.
Gender not stated in the corpus, so written neutral (they/them).
An earlier draft said "Leila, 58, shift supervisor, hypertension + type 2 diabetes".
None of that was supported. Corrected — see C-05 and C-06 in the verification log.
